entry.title: EMBL alumnus Nishit Goradia on building a research career in Poland

media:group.media:title: EMBL alumnus Nishit Goradia on building a research career in Poland
media:group.media:description:
EMBL Hamburg alumnus Nishit Goradia recently moved to Warsaw to start his own research group at the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IMol PAS) in Warsaw. Building on his postdoctoral work in integrative structural biology and cancer, he plans to shift to cell biology and investigate the molecular mechanisms of transcriptional regulation through protein assembly. He remains connected to the EMBL network and is interested in collaborating with fellow alumni in Warsaw.
The video was recorded during the EMBL in Poland event in September 2026. The meeting served as a platform to build bridges and share the latest research, as well as services and training opportunities at EMBL.

entry.title: New AI tools for biology rely on open data

media:group.media:title: New AI tools for biology rely on open data
media:group.media:description:
Good AI models require lots of high-quality training data. EMBL-EBI Interim Director, Jo McEntyre explains how high-quality datasets from open data resources, such as those managed by EMBL-EBI, support the development of new AI models for biology.
In this video, McEntyre shares: - How open datasets power breakthroughs like AlphaFold, developed by Google DeepMind to predict protein structures; - How the AlphaFold Database makes over 200 million structure predictions freely accessible worldwide; - How AI is accelerating data curation and enabling curators to annotate more records than ever before.
Learn more: AI at EMBL: https://www.embl.org/topics/ai-at-embl/

entry.title: Urszula McClurg on the impact of EMBL facilities on her research

media:group.media:title: Urszula McClurg on the impact of EMBL facilities on her research
media:group.media:description:
Urszula McClurg is relocating her research group from the University of Liverpool to the Institute of Medical Biology of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IMB PAS) in Łódź. She has received an EMBO Installation Grant as well as funding from the Polish government to study meiotic genes and their role in cancer. Her group’s work depends heavily on proteomics, and access to EMBL's Proteomics Core Facility has been essential. She believes the connection with EMBL and EMBO is very beneficial to scientists and wishes for it to develop further across Poland.

entry.title: The Trivedi Group studies the first steps of life using stem-cell-derived models | EMBL Barcelona

media:group.media:title: The Trivedi Group studies the first steps of life using stem-cell-derived models | EMBL Barcelona
media:group.media:description:
The Trivedi group aims to understand the self-organisation of cells, fundamental to metazoan development, through comparative study of embryos and organoids that generate a global coordinate system de novo.
How do tissues reliably form complex shapes and patterns in multicellular animals? Using aggregates of embryonic stem cells from mouse, human, and other models, the Trivedi group recreates early developmental events in the lab. By probing how mechanochemical coupling between cells interacts with metabolic constraints, researchers uncover fundamental rules guiding robust symmetry breaking and tissue patterning during the earliest stages of development.
Inspired by the role of metabolism in mammalian stem cell aggregates, the Trivedi group looks into nutrient regulation of the cell cycle and explores how it could have contributed to the emergence of multicellularity.
Building on studies of multicellular self-organisation, researchers at the Trivedi group explore how environmental changes such as temperature extremes impact robust tissue development in ectothermic embryos like zebrafish.
To tackle biological complexity, the group develops software and hardware tools, including machine learning algorithms for high-throughput imaging/analysis of organoids, methods to map mechanical properties in stem cell and lab automation solutions to improve experimental reproducibility.

entry.title: We are EMBL: Emily Bowler-Barnett - Senior Database Curator and Product Manager

media:group.media:title: We are EMBL: Emily Bowler-Barnett - Senior Database Curator and Product Manager
media:group.media:description:
EMBL employs researchers and skilled professionals from around the world. Emily Bowler-Barnett is a Senior Database Curator and Product Manager at EMBL-EBI, near Cambridge UK.
Emily works on UniProt, the world’s leading open-access database for protein sequences. UniProt is similar to a dictionary for proteins and their function.
As a biocurator, Emily reads scientific publication and uses her specialist knowledge to curate relevant data into specialist databases. She also coordinates much of the training and teaching for biologists and bioinformaticians who use UniProt. Emily works closely with the website team to implement new features and improvements, and manages the communications and social media for her team.
Emily’s hobbies include strength training, architectural photography, and training her dog Nettie, named after American geneticist Nettie Stevens.
UniProt is jointly run by teams at EMBL-EBI, the Swiss Institute for Bioinformatics (SIB), and the Protein Information Resource (PIR).

entry.title: The Bernabeu Group studies cerebral malaria on-a-chip | EMBL Barcelona

media:group.media:title: The Bernabeu Group studies cerebral malaria on-a-chip | EMBL Barcelona
media:group.media:description:
The Bernabeu group aims to understand the mechanisms that lead to vascular dysfunction in cerebral malaria by developing new in vitro models of the human blood-brain barrier.
The blood-brain barrier (BBB) plays a key role in maintaining neural function, as it prevents the entry of toxins and infectious agents into the brain parenchyma. The highly specialised function of the BBB is accomplished by the establishment of endothelial tight junctions and transporters that provide refined control of the paracellular and transcellular permeability. BBB disruption has been associated with multiple severe diseases, including malaria. Plasmodium spp. cause around 200 million new malaria infections and half a million deaths every year. Among the multiple severe complications that malaria patients can suffer, cerebral malaria is one of the deadliest.

entry.title: EMBL Barcelona researchers build tissues to understand them

media:group.media:title: EMBL Barcelona researchers build tissues to understand them
media:group.media:description:
Scientists at EMBL Barcelona focus on tissue biology and disease modelling.
Molecular biology underpins our understanding of life, but the human body is more than just a collection of incredible molecules and fascinating cell types. The correct functioning of our bodies also depends on a higher level of organisation: how millions of different cells interact with each other – chemically, physically and dynamically – to form healthy tissues and organs.
